passage: Sunday afternoon in Jaya's rented room in Hyderabad, and nothing was due. She lay on the bed for ten minutes, then sat up, heart thumping. Lazy. She opened her laptop, closed it, reorganised her pens, and felt worse. Her friend Darshan, dropping off a borrowed book, found her pacing. 'You look like you're waiting for an exam result,' he said. 'I'm just wasting the day.' Darshan shrugged. 'Remember last month? You studied every single Sunday and fell asleep in the practical.' Jaya remembered. They walked to the lake, ate roasted corn and said nothing much. On Monday she finished her lab report in half the usual time and noticed, with surprise, that she didn't mind.

qa.q: What did Jaya and Darshan eat by the lake?
qa.a: Roasted corn.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she lay on the bed with nothing due?
qa.a: She felt guilty and anxious, calling herself lazy, so the rest felt empty rather than restful.

qa.q: What helped Jaya see rest differently?
qa.a: Darshan reminded her that overwork had left her asleep in the practical, and after a real break she finished her report faster, showing rest improves later work.

qa.q: How did Darshan see Jaya's pacing?
qa.a: He saw that she was stressed, not resting, and gently reminded her of last month.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels lazy and anxious whenever not being productive, and learns that genuine rest makes later work better.

passage:
The office had emptied when Arohi, his teammate, stopped at Jatin's desk.
'Jatin, it's nine. Why are you still here?'
'Just finishing the slides.'
'You finished them at six. I saw.'
'Then I'll check the numbers again.' Jatin rubbed his eyes. 'If I go home I'll just sit there feeling useless.'
'Useless how?'
'Last Sunday I watched a film and spent the whole time thinking I should be working. Couldn't enjoy a minute.'
'You know your best pitch was the week after Holi, when you'd taken four days off?'
'That was luck.'
'Was it? You were sharp. You laughed in meetings.'
Jatin went quiet. 'So rest is... part of the work?'
'It's what makes the work good. Go home. Take a walk. Leave the laptop shut.'
He saved the file and, slowly, closed it.

qa.q: When did Jatin actually finish the slides?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel while watching a film last Sunday?
qa.a: He felt guilty and anxious, thinking he should be working, so he couldn't enjoy the rest.

qa.q: What turned Jatin's thinking around?
qa.a: Arohi reminded him that his best pitch came after four days off, helping him see rest as part of doing good work.

qa.q: How does Arohi see Jatin staying late?
qa.a: Arohi sees it as unnecessary and worrying, since the slides were done, and cares enough to send Jatin home.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels useless and guilty whenever not working, and a teammate who helps him see that recovery makes later work better.

passage:
'Tanvir, it's Sunday. Why are you ironing your formal shirt at nine?'
'Thought I'd go to the library.'
'You finished the assignment last night.'
'I know. But if I sit around, I feel like a loser. Everyone's doing internships.'
'You sat around yesterday for ten minutes and kept checking your phone for emails.'
'That's the thing. Even when I rest, I'm not resting. My chest feels tight.'
'Come to the lake with me. No phone. Two hours.'
'And then?'
'Then you study tonight with a brain that works.'
At the lake Tanvir kept reaching for his pocket. By the second hour he was skimming stones and laughing at Amandeep's terrible throws.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep invite Tanvir to go?
qa.a: To the lake, with no phone, for two hours.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir feel like a loser when he rests?
qa.a: He feels anxious and guilty, as if resting means falling behind everyone doing internships.

qa.q: What did Amandeep suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Two phone-free hours at the lake, so Tanvir's rest is real and his brain works better when he studies later.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Tanvir ironing a shirt on Sunday?
qa.a: Amandeep probably finds it worrying and a bit sad to see a friend who cannot switch off.

grounding: A young adult who feels lazy whenever not working finds rest anxious until a friend shows that recovery helps later work.

passage: For most of second year, a voice in my head said 'Lazy' whenever I sat still. I'm Sangeeta, and I'd lie down after classes and immediately start listing what I hadn't done. Rest felt empty and anxious, so I stopped resting at all. By March I was reading chapters three times and remembering nothing. My friend Nikita, a swimmer, laughed at me kindly. 'You think our coach makes us train every day? Rest days are when muscles actually grow.' I tried it: Saturday evenings off, no guilt allowed. For the first few weeks I kept checking the clock. Now I go up to the terrace with tea, and on Monday my notes make sense again.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta do on Saturday evenings now?
qa.a: Goes up to the terrace with tea.

qa.q: How did rest feel to Sangeeta during second year?
qa.a: Rest felt empty and anxious, with a guilty voice calling Sangeeta lazy.

qa.q: What helped Sangeeta rest without guilt?
qa.a: Nikita's point that rest days are when muscles grow, and a fixed Saturday evening off.

qa.q: How might Nikita see Sangeeta's habit of never resting?
qa.a: Nikita sees it kindly but clearly, as a swimmer who knows rest is part of getting stronger.

grounding: A student who feels lazy when not productive learns that recovery makes later work better.

passage:
Supervisor's note, internship review, week 6
Payal is one of our most careful interns, but I have noticed a pattern. She logs in on weekends, answers messages at midnight, and on the one day I insisted she take off, she came in 'just for an hour' and stayed till seven. In our review she admitted that resting makes her feel guilty and jittery, as if she is being lazy. Her work this week had small errors she would never usually make. I told her plainly that recovery is part of good work, not a break from it. We agreed she will not log in on Sundays, and I will not message her then either. I will check in with her next week.
Ujjwal

qa.q: What did Payal and Ujjwal agree about Sundays?
qa.a: Payal will not log in on Sundays, and Ujjwal will not message then either.

qa.q: How does Payal feel when she rests?
qa.a: She feels guilty and jittery, as if resting means being lazy.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal also promise not to message on Sundays?
qa.a: So Payal could rest fully without pressure, showing that recovery is valued as part of good work.

qa.q: What would change if Ujjwal praised Payal's weekend work instead?
qa.a: Payal's guilt about resting would grow, and the small errors from tiredness would likely increase.

grounding: A supervisor sees a young intern who feels guilty resting and helps her accept recovery as part of good work.

passage:
Sunday, 6 p.m.
I lay on my bed from two to five today and I still feel guilty writing that. Three hours. The whole time a voice in my head kept listing things: the internship form, the stats notes, the gym. So I wasn't really resting, just lying there anxious, scrolling, calling myself lazy. Rehana came in with chai and said, "You rested, na? Good." I said I'd wasted the afternoon. She laughed and said her swimming coach used to say muscles grow on rest days, not in the pool. I've been thinking about that. Last week I didn't stop at all, and by Friday I couldn't write one clean paragraph. Next Sunday I'm going to try it properly: phone in the drawer, a walk by the lake, no list. And no apologising.
Chandrika

qa.q: What did Rehana's swimming coach used to say?
qa.a: That muscles grow on rest days, not in the pool.

qa.q: Why couldn't Chandrika enjoy the three hours of rest?
qa.a: Chandrika felt guilty and anxious, with a voice listing tasks and calling rest lazy.

qa.q: What does Chandrika plan to do differently next Sunday, and why might it help?
qa.a: Put the phone in a drawer, walk by the lake and drop the list, so rest actually restores and later work improves.

qa.q: How does Rehana see Chandrika's afternoon?
qa.a: Rehana sees it as healthy rest worth celebrating, not a waste, and brings chai to say so.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels lazy whenever not productive finding rest empty and anxious, and beginning to see that recovery makes later work better.
